facts.statement: Linear programming is a set of mathematical techniques to allocate limited resources among competing demands in an optimal way. The function to be maximised or minimised (profit, loss, time, cost) is the objective function; the conditions it must satisfy are the constraints; and the variables whose values are to be determined are the decision variables. Typical constraints come from working capital requirements, the market not absorbing the whole output, capacity, labour availability and raw materials.

A problem can be formulated as a linear programme if: all relations are linear (proportional: if 4 persons produce one unit, 12 are needed for 3 units); the constraints are known and deterministic (probabilities of occurrence presumed to be 1); the variables are non-negative; and the decision variables are divisible.

The graphical approach suits two decision variables. For the courseware's radio (x) and television (y) problem the constraints are 3x + y <= 10 (machine time), x + y <= 4 (assembly time), x + 4y <= 12 (cash, from 1,000x + 4,000y <= 12,000) and x, y >= 0, with objective: maximise profit 1,000x + 2,000y. Each constraint is drawn as a line, and points on or below it satisfy it.

The set of points satisfying all the constraints together (here a pentagon ABCDE in the first quadrant) is the set of feasible solutions. Any feasible point such as x = y = 0 is feasible, but the aim is the feasible point with the highest profit. An iso-profit line joins the combinations that give the same profit (for profit 1,000x + 2,000y two radios earn what one television earns, so its slope is -1/2). Moving the iso-profit line away from the origin as far as it still touches the feasible region identifies the optimum at the last vertex touched. In the courseware the optimum is point D, 4/3 radios and 8/3 televisions, where the assembly and cash constraints are binding (fully used) and machine time has surplus capacity.

If an optimal solution exists, at least one optimal solution lies at an extreme point (vertex) of the polygon of feasible solutions, and since there are only finitely many vertices the maximum profit can be found by evaluating them. The only exception is when the iso-profit line has the same slope as a boundary line, in which case there are many optimal solutions with the same profit along that line. If integer solutions are required one settles for the next best. The drawback of the graphical approach is that with many constraints there are many points to evaluate.

The simplex method is the standard technique for optimisation problems with an objective function and several constraints expressed as inequalities. In standard form each constraint is converted into an equation by adding a slack variable (non-negative), and the right-hand sides must be non-negative; the objective is written as Z - c1 x1 - ... = 0. A tableau lists the basic variables, the coefficients of Z and the variables, and the solution column.

Simplex iteration for a maximisation problem: the entering variable is the one with the most negative coefficient in the Z-row; the variable to be replaced (leaving variable) is found by dividing each solution value by the corresponding positive entry in the entering column and choosing the smallest positive ratio; the pivot entry is where this row and column meet; the new pivot row is the current pivot row divided by the pivot entry; every other row becomes current row minus (its entry in the pivot column) times the new pivot row. Repeat until there is no negative number in the Z-row. For minimisation the steps are identical, but a positive Z-row entry indicates improvement and the entering variable has the largest positive value.

facts.statement: The courseware's example maximises Z = 2B + 4C (bats and chess sets) subject to 4B + 6C <= 120, 2B + 6C <= 72, C <= 10 and B, C >= 0. After slack variables m, n and p, three tableaux give Z = 40 (C enters, p leaves), Z = 52 (B enters, n leaves) and Z = 64 (p enters, m leaves), with B = 24 and C = 4 at the optimum. A positive slack in the optimum tableau means that resource is not fully used (abundant); a slack equal to zero means the resource is fully used (scarce). In the optimum tableau the basic variables are p (= 6), B (= 24) and C (= 4), so the unused capacity is in the third workshop (C <= 10 with C = 4), while the first two workshops are fully used; the courseware text says instead that m = 6 and that workshop 1 is not fully used.

In the optimum tableau of the courseware example the Z-row coefficients under the slack variables of the two fully used workshops are 1/3 each and under the slack of the unused one is 0, so one more unit of a scarce resource adds that amount to the objective (Z-row coefficient of a slack variable = shadow price of its resource). payload.title: What a linear programme is, and when it applies
payload.core_explanation_md:
Linear programming decides **how much of each activity to do** when resources are limited, so as to get the best possible result.

| Part | Meaning | Banking example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Decision variables** | The quantities to be decided | Number of home loans and vehicle loans to process |
| **Objective function** | The measure to maximise or minimise | Total profit, or total cost |
| **Constraints** | Limits the plan must respect | Officer hours, documentation hours, funds available |
| **Non-negativity** | Variables cannot be below zero | You cannot process minus five loans |

For the method to apply, four conditions must hold: everything is **linear** (double the activity, double the use of resource and the profit), data are **known and certain**, variables are **non-negative**, and activity levels are **divisible**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: If profit per unit falls as volume rises, or if a resource requirement is uncertain, a plain linear programme is not the right model. The divisibility condition is why you may get an answer like 2.67 loans: round it with care, or use a method for whole numbers.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank's profit per loan drops by half once more than 50 loans are processed. Which LP condition fails?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Linearity (proportionality): profit per unit is not constant, so the objective is not linear in the number of loans.

payload.title: Formulating a problem: a four-step checklist
payload.core_explanation_md:
Turn the words into mathematics in this order:

1. **Name the decision variables** (x = home loans per week, y = vehicle loans per week).
2. **Write the objective** as a linear function (profit 4x + 3y, in Rs thousand).
3. **Write one constraint per limited resource**: resource used by all activities is at most (or at least) what is available. Home loans need 3 officer-hours and vehicle loans 2: 3x + 2y is at most 120.
4. **Add non-negativity**: x and y are at least 0.

Each "at most" constraint is a ceiling, each "at least" constraint a floor. Units must match on both sides.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A common slip is a constraint that mixes units (hours on the left, rupees on the right) or a missing non-negativity condition, which lets the model choose a negative quantity.

self_check.prompt_text: Documentation takes 1 hour per home loan and 2 hours per vehicle loan, with 60 hours available. Write the constraint.

payload.title: The graphical method: feasible region and corner points
payload.core_explanation_md:
With two decision variables you can draw the problem.

1. Draw each constraint as a line. Shade the side that satisfies it.
2. The overlap of all shaded sides (in the first quadrant) is the **feasible region**: every point in it is a plan that obeys all the limits.
3. Draw an **iso-profit line**: all the combinations that earn the same profit. Slide it away from the origin, keeping its slope, until it is about to leave the region.
4. The last point touched is the **optimum**. It is a **corner (extreme point)** of the region.

Because an optimum is always at a corner (if it exists), you can skip the sliding and simply **evaluate the objective at each corner** and pick the best.

Exception: if the iso-profit line is parallel to a boundary, every point on that edge is optimal: many solutions with the same profit.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: At the optimum corner, the constraints that meet there are fully used (binding). The others usually have spare room.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is it enough to check only the corner points?
self_check.expected_takeaway: If an optimum exists, at least one lies at a corner of the feasible region, and there are only a few corners.

payload.title: Standard form for the simplex method: slack variables
payload.core_explanation_md:
The simplex method works on equations, not inequalities. So turn every "at most" constraint into an equation by adding a **slack variable**: the unused part of the resource.

3x + 2y is at most 120 becomes 3x + 2y + s1 = 120, with s1 at least 0.

The objective Z = 4x + 3y is rewritten Z - 4x - 3y = 0. All variables, including slacks, are non-negative, and each right-hand side must be non-negative.

The starting plan is "do nothing": x = 0, y = 0, so each slack equals the whole resource (s1 = 120) and Z = 0. The first **tableau** is a table of these equations with a row for each constraint and a Z-row.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A slack of zero at the end means that resource has been completely used; a positive slack means some is left over.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a slack variable measure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The amount of a resource left unused.

payload.title: One simplex iteration, in five moves
payload.core_explanation_md:
For a **maximisation**, repeat these moves until the Z-row has no negative numbers:

| Move | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| 1. **Entering variable** | The column with the most negative Z-row entry (the best profit gain per unit) |
| 2. **Leaving variable** | For each row with a positive entry in that column, divide the solution value by that entry. The smallest ratio picks the row |
| 3. **Pivot entry** | Where the entering column meets the leaving row |
| 4. **New pivot row** | Divide the leaving row by the pivot entry |
| 5. **Other rows** (including Z) | Subtract (the row's entry in the entering column) times the new pivot row |

The smallest-ratio rule stops you from pushing a variable so far that some resource would go negative.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Each iteration moves to a neighbouring corner of the feasible region with a profit at least as high. When no negative remains in the Z-row, no neighbouring corner is better.

self_check.prompt_text: Solution values 120 and 60, entering-column entries 3 and 1. Which row leaves?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ratios 40 and 60: the smaller is 40, so the first row leaves.

payload.title: Reading the final tableau: scarce and abundant resources, shadow prices
payload.core_explanation_md:
The last tableau tells you far more than the plan.

- **Basic variables** and the solution column give the optimal quantities and the maximum Z.
- A **slack variable that is basic with a positive value** marks an **abundant** resource: some is left over, so more of it would not help.
- A **slack equal to zero** marks a **scarce** resource: it is fully used and limits the profit.
- The Z-row entry under a slack variable is the **shadow price** of that resource: how much Z would rise for one more unit of it. Abundant resources have a shadow price of zero.

This is how a manager decides where extra capacity or funds would pay off.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Always read the slack from the tableau itself, not from memory of the problem: check the basic variables and their values. The courseware example illustrates why. Its final tableau has the slack of the third workshop equal to 6, but the accompanying text attributes the slack to the first workshop.

self_check.prompt_text: Optimum tableau: basic variables are x = 30, y = 15 and s3 = 25; the slack entries in the Z-row are 1.25, 0.25 and 0. Which resources are scarce, and what is each extra unit of the first worth?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The first two resources (their slacks are zero, non-basic) are scarce; the third (s3 = 25) is abundant. An extra unit of the first resource adds 1.25 to Z.

payload.title: Minimisation, and what else linear programming does
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Spreadsheets can solve problems with ten or more variables, so the hand methods are for understanding, not for large models.

self_check.prompt_text: In a minimisation, which Z-row entry picks the entering variable?
